A person who has met with foul play is a more complex and more serious matter, and the investigation of such cases requires, correspondingly, more thorough and more rigorous methods. The scene of the crime — if scene there be, and in many cases of foul play there is no single identifiable scene — must be examined with the greatest possible care and completeness, since the physical evidence available at the scene is typically the most direct and least ambiguous evidence available, before it has been contaminated by subsequent handling or disturbed by the passage of time.

I have made it a practice, in cases involving suspected foul play, to insist upon examining the relevant scene as early as possible and with as little prior disturbance as can be arranged. The scene of a crime is a document that deteriorates with time — not merely through the active contamination that results from the presence of multiple investigators and their various activities, but through the natural processes of physical degradation that begin to operate upon any physical evidence the moment the crime is committed and do not cease until the evidence is either preserved by some deliberate act or destroyed by time. The investigator who arrives at a scene twenty-four hours after the crime was committed is working with considerably less information than the one who arrives within an hour, and the difference is not always recoverable.

The footprint evidence, of which I have made considerable professional use, is particularly susceptible to deterioration. A footprint in soft earth or mud that is perfectly clear and detailed at the moment of its making will be measurably degraded within a few hours by the action of rain, wind, and the ordinary settling of the soil. The specific features of the print — the pattern of the sole, the depth and character of the heel-strike, the particulars of the toe-off — that allow the trained observer to extract information about the person who made the print are precisely the features that are most rapidly lost as the environmental conditions act upon the physical medium. I have accordingly developed the practice of making, at the very outset of any field investigation, a complete photographic and analytical record of all footprint evidence present at the scene, before proceeding to any other aspect of the examination.

The chemistry of the investigation extends beyond the laboratory and into the field. Many of the most important types of physical evidence are chemical in character — the traces of various substances on surfaces, in fabrics, on skin; the products of combustion that indicate the nature of the fuel burned and the conditions of the burning; the biological materials that can indicate the identity of the person who left them and the circumstances under which they were left. My training in analytical chemistry has been essential to my ability to identify and interpret this class of evidence, and I have spent considerable effort in recent years developing and refining techniques for the field analysis of chemical evidence that do not require the transport of samples to the laboratory.

The study of documents — their paper, their ink, their handwriting, their physical condition — constitutes another major branch of the investigative science, and one in which I have taken a particular professional interest. The physical characteristics of a document encode a great deal of information that is independent of the document's textual content: information about the period and place of the document's creation, about the instruments and materials used in its creation, about the physical history of the document since its creation, and about the conditions under which it was most recently handled. A letter that appears, on its face, to be a perfectly ordinary communication between two ordinary persons may, when its physical characteristics are properly examined, reveal that it was written on paper that was not commercially available at the time it purports to have been written, with ink that was not in common use in the country where it purports to have been written, by a person whose handwriting shows the characteristics of controlled simulation rather than the natural variation of spontaneous composition.

Forgery is a subject that repays careful study, both because it is in itself a common form of criminal enterprise and because the study of forgery illuminates, by contrast, the nature of genuine documents. The forger who works with skill and care is attempting to reproduce the appearance of authenticity — to create an object that will pass, upon examination, for something that it is not. To do this successfully, the forger must understand what genuine authenticity looks like — must know, that is, the specific physical characteristics that distinguish a genuine document of the purported type and period from an imitation. In attempting to reproduce these characteristics, the skilled forger demonstrates, paradoxically, that the characteristics themselves are real and specific and identifiable — because if they were not, there would be nothing specific to imitate. The forger's art is thus a kind of tribute to the reality of the physical evidences of authenticity, and the study of forgery is an indirect way of studying the nature of those evidences.

The art of disguise, which I have cultivated as a professional tool to an extent that Watson has occasionally found surprising, operates on similar principles. A convincing disguise is not merely a matter of altering the superficial features of appearance — the colour of the hair, the style of the beard, the cut of the clothing. It is a matter of inhabiting a different physical character: of adopting the posture, the gait, the characteristic gestures, the vocal qualities, and the social manners of the person being impersonated. The physical body is a document that the trained observer reads continuously, and a disguise that alters only the textual content while leaving the physical sub-text intact is a disguise that will not survive close examination by anyone who knows what to look for.

I have found, in the practice of disguise, that the most important element is not the alteration of the appearance but the alteration of the habitual self — the suppression of the physical habits and mannerisms that characterise one's normal presence and the substitution for them of the physical habits and mannerisms appropriate to the assumed identity. This is a more demanding exercise than is generally supposed, and it requires a kind of physical self-knowledge that most people have never had occasion to develop: the ability to observe one's own characteristic physical habits from the outside, as it were, and to consciously suppress and replace them.

The great city of London, in the years of my most active practice, was undergoing a transformation that was visible in the physical fabric of the streets as well as in the social composition of the population that inhabited them. The older buildings of an earlier century were being replaced, district by district, by the newer construction of the Victorian era: wider streets, more uniform building lines, better sanitation, and a general regularisation of the urban fabric that made the city more navigable but, in certain respects, less interesting to the close observer. The older, more irregular districts — the warrens of streets and courts and alleys that had grown up organically over centuries, without plan or systematic oversight — retained a complexity and a character that the newer development, for all its hygienic and practical advantages, could not entirely match.

I knew those older districts with an intimacy that I had acquired through years of deliberate exploration, and I found them consistently more informative than the newer, more regular areas of the city. The complexity of their geography mirrored, in some way, the complexity of their social life: they were places where the conventional social categories and the conventional social hierarchies were less rigorously enforced, where the established and the marginal, the respectable and the disreputable, existed in a closer and more complicated relationship than was possible in the more formally organised residential areas. And it was in these zones of social complexity that much of the most interesting criminal activity of the city was concentrated — not merely because they provided convenient cover, but because they existed at the intersection of social worlds that normally kept themselves separate, and criminal enterprise has always depended upon the exploitation of exactly that kind of intersection.

The professional criminal of the higher type — the organiser, the planner, the architect of extended schemes — tends to inhabit a social position that straddles the legitimate and the illegitimate, presenting a respectable face to the world while conducting, beneath that face, activities of a very different character. The perfect cover for a receiver of stolen goods is a legitimate dealer in second-hand goods; the perfect cover for a fraudster operating on a large scale is a position of genuine business respectability from which the fraudulent operations can be conducted under the shelter of the legitimate ones. The investigator who approaches such a person looking only for the criminal and ignoring the legitimate will often miss the evidence that matters, because it is in the relationship between the legitimate and the illegitimate operations — in the specific points of contact between the two, in the ways in which the criminal activity is concealed within or enabled by the legitimate one — that the most revealing evidence is typically to be found.



~ ~ ~

Watson has sometimes observed, with the gentle persistence that characterises his friendship, that my approach to the human beings involved in the cases I investigate is insufficiently attentive to their emotional experience. I understand his point, and I do not entirely dismiss it, though I think it reflects a misunderstanding of the nature of the investigative enterprise rather than a genuine deficiency in my character. The investigator's primary obligation is to the truth of what happened, and the emotional experience of the people involved, while it is part of the truth, is only part of it — and often not the part that most urgently requires attention.

There is, moreover, a practical reason for maintaining a degree of emotional distance from the specific situations under investigation: the investigator who becomes emotionally entangled with the circumstances of a case loses, to the extent of that entanglement, the objectivity that makes accurate analysis possible. I have seen this happen with other investigators — good men, conscientious and intelligent, whose emotional involvement with particular clients or particular situations led them to read the evidence in ways that served their emotional commitments rather than the truth, and to miss or minimise the evidence that pointed in uncomfortable directions. It is a consistent and serious professional failure, and it is one that I have worked consistently to avoid.

This does not mean that I am indifferent to the suffering of the people who come to me. On the contrary: it is precisely because I am not indifferent to their suffering that I maintain the discipline required to investigate their cases accurately rather than comfortingly. The person who needs the truth of their situation — the correct identification of the danger they face, the genuine assessment of the evidence against or for them, the accurate reconstruction of what actually happened rather than what they would prefer to have happened — is not well served by an investigator who has allowed his sympathies to cloud his judgement. They are served by an investigator who cares enough about their wellbeing to remain honest even when honesty is uncomfortable.

The cases that have tested this discipline most severely are those in which the truth, when discovered, is not what the client wished or expected. The wife who suspected her husband of fraud and was correct, but had not anticipated discovering that the fraud involved the systematic deception and financial ruin of people she knew and respected. The parent who feared that their child was in danger, and was correct, but had not anticipated that the danger was of a character that reflected very poorly on their own conduct as a parent. The business partner who suspected theft, and was correct, but had not anticipated that the theft was enabled by a flaw in their own practices that they had been systematically failing to address. In all of these cases, the truth, though it was the truth the client came to me to discover, was not entirely the truth they wanted.

I have developed, over the years, a certain technique for the delivery of unwelcome truths — a technique that involves neither the softening of the essential fact nor the unnecessary amplification of the painful elements, but the presentation of the truth in a context that makes its practical implications clear and that points, where possible, toward constructive responses. The truth delivered without context or without practical direction is a form of cruelty; the truth delivered with a clear account of what follows from it and what can be done in response to it is a form of genuine help. I aim for the latter, though I do not always achieve it to the degree that Watson's standards of human sympathy would require.

The observation of the human face is a science in itself, and one that I have studied with considerable thoroughness, though I have found that its results are less reliable than the observation of the physical environment or of physical objects, precisely because the face is the most consciously managed part of the human person's external presentation. People learn, from early childhood, to manage their facial expressions in response to social expectations — to display appropriate emotional responses and to suppress inappropriate ones — and the result is that the face, in social situations, reflects what the person believes they should be feeling or wishes to be seen as feeling at least as much as it reflects what they are actually feeling.

The more reliable indicators of the actual emotional and psychological state are, as I have noted, the hands and the body as a whole — the physical posture, the pattern of movement, the management of the breath and the muscular tension that are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and therefore not susceptible to the same degree of conscious management as the facial expression. A person who has trained themselves to maintain a perfectly controlled and socially appropriate facial expression will often betray, through the tightening of the hands on a handbag handle, or through the slightly increased rate and shallowness of the breathing, or through the particular way in which they hold their shoulders, the emotional reality that the face is working to conceal.

I should note here, in the interest of completeness, that the observation of these non-facial indicators is a skill that must be applied with considerable care, because the interpretation of bodily signals is subject to all the errors of interpretation that affect the reading of any kind of evidence. A person who appears tense and anxious in my sitting room may be tense and anxious because they have recently committed a crime and are afraid of detection; or they may be tense and anxious because they are consulting a detective and are self-conscious about what the detective may observe about them; or they may be tense and anxious for reasons entirely unrelated to the matter at hand — a difficult family situation, a financial worry, a physical discomfort. The correct interpretation of the observed signal requires the accumulation of all the available evidence and the careful consideration of all the possible explanations, not the simple matching of signal to conclusion.

The winter of my most productive years as a consulting detective brought a particular variety of case to Baker Street with unusual frequency: cases arising from the intersection of the old wealth of the English upper classes with the new money of the commercial and industrial expansion of the era. The specific form that these cases typically took was the exposure of fraud — the systematic exploitation, by persons of sharp intelligence and no scruples, of the credulity and the financial inexperience of persons who had recently come into money through inheritance or commercial success and who were now subject to the attentions of the various categories of swindler and confidence operator who cluster around new money with the predictability of any other natural phenomenon responding to the availability of its preferred resource.

The variety of the schemes was considerable, though the underlying structure was in most cases similar: the establishment of false credibility, the cultivation of trust, the creation of an apparently irresistible opportunity, and the disappearance with the money before the victim had time to investigate what they had actually invested in. The sophistication of the scheme varied with the intelligence and resources of the operator, from the crude but sometimes effective confidence trick of the common swindler to the elaborate and technically competent frauds mounted by operators who had made a serious professional study of finance and law specifically in order to exploit their knowledge for criminal purposes.

I have a particular professional admiration — or at any rate, a particular professional interest — for the fraudster of the higher type, the man or woman who brings to the design and execution of a large-scale financial crime the same qualities of intelligence, planning, and systematic method that I bring to its detection. The relationship between the skilled criminal and the skilled investigator is, in some respects, an adversarial one between practitioners of the same craft applied to opposite ends, and the investigation of crimes committed by criminals of genuine ability has the quality, for me, of a test of the method against a worthy opponent.

I say worthy opponent, not admirable person. The distinction is important. The intelligence and the skill that a talented criminal brings to the business of deception and theft are real qualities, and I acknowledge them as such; but they are qualities in the service of purposes that cause real harm to real people, and the harm is not diminished by the elegance with which it is accomplished. I have encountered criminals whom, in other circumstances, I might have found interesting companions; I have found none whom I could regard as admirable, because the combination of genuine intelligence with the deliberate choice to apply it to the suffering of others seems to me to represent a specific form of moral failure that no degree of technical brilliance can redeem.

The long evenings at Baker Street, during the periods between active cases, were given over to a variety of activities that Watson has documented with varying degrees of accuracy. The chemical experiments have been described. The monographs — which represent my most systematic attempt to place the science of criminal investigation on a proper theoretical foundation — absorbed many hours that Watson observed without fully understanding their purpose, since the connections between the specific topics I was investigating and the practical problems of criminal detection were not always immediately apparent.

The monograph on the varieties of tobacco ash was the most immediately practical of the series, since the identification of tobacco residue is a common problem in the investigation of crimes committed in environments where smoking occurs — which is, in practice, a very high proportion of all environments. The characteristic ash produced by the combustion of different varieties of tobacco differs in colour, texture, and chemical composition in ways that are consistent and reproducible enough to serve as reliable identifying markers, once a sufficiently extensive reference collection has been assembled and the distinguishing characteristics of each variety have been systematically documented. The assembly of the reference collection required years of patient work and the cooperation of a considerable number of tobacconists and fellow-smokers; the documentation of the distinguishing characteristics required extensive chemical analysis and the development of several new analytical techniques. The result was, I believe, a genuinely useful contribution to the forensic sciences, though it has not yet received the recognition in English-speaking countries that it has achieved on the Continent.

The other monographs addressed questions that were, in some cases, more recondite but that I judged to be of practical importance in specific classes of investigation. The study of the typefaces of the principal London printing-houses grew out of a case in which the identification of a forged document depended on the identification of the specific printing-house that had produced the typeface used in its production; the monograph on the distinguishing features of one hundred and forty varieties of ink grew out of another. In each case, the theoretical study was motivated by practical necessity, and the practical application confirmed the utility of the theoretical work.

Watson has sometimes expressed puzzlement at the degree of specialised knowledge that I bring to specific investigative problems — at the fact that I appear to have, in immediate readiness, expertise in subjects that seem, at first glance, to be of no conceivable practical utility. His puzzlement reflects a failure to appreciate the specific character of the investigative problem, which is that the investigator cannot know in advance what information will be required for any particular case and must therefore maintain a readiness across a very wide range of subjects. The knowledge that has no apparent utility today may be the essential knowledge of tomorrow's case, and the investigator who has not maintained it will be at a disadvantage that cannot be easily remedied on short notice.

I have accordingly made it a practice to read widely and to retain carefully, storing away, in the organised catalogues of my memory, information whose immediate utility is not apparent but whose relevance to some future problem I judge to be plausible. The brain, as I have observed to Watson on more than one occasion, is not an infinitely capacious storage system, and the indiscriminate accumulation of information about every conceivable subject would be not merely impractical but actively counterproductive, since the genuinely useful information would be buried under the weight of the irrelevant. The discipline lies in the selection — in the development of the professional judgement that allows the investigator to determine, in advance, what categories of knowledge are likely to be relevant to the types of problem they will encounter, and to focus their acquisitive reading and study on those categories.

The geography of London — its streets, its districts, its social topography, the specific character of its various neighbourhoods and the ways in which that character has changed and continues to change over time — is obviously among the most important categories of knowledge for an investigator operating primarily in the metropolitan area. I have walked every significant street in the city at some point in my career, and many of them I have walked repeatedly, in different conditions and at different hours, specifically for the purpose of maintaining and updating my practical knowledge of the city's physical and social character. This knowledge has been of service in more cases than I can readily enumerate: it has allowed me to identify the area from which a client or a suspect has come from small physical traces, to predict the routes that criminals have taken in the course of their operations, to identify the types of business and institution present in specific areas and the potential significance of their presence or absence to specific investigations.



~ ~ ~

The relationship between criminal activity and the social and economic conditions in which it occurs is a subject that I have considered at considerable length, not out of any sociological or political interest, but because the understanding of this relationship is directly relevant to the practical work of criminal investigation. A crime does not occur in a vacuum; it occurs in a specific social and economic environment, and the characteristics of that environment shape and constrain the types of crime that occur within it, the specific methods that criminals employ, the specific vulnerabilities that they exploit, and the specific traces that they leave behind. The investigator who does not understand these relationships will be at a systematic disadvantage in interpreting the evidence they encounter.

The poverty of the worst areas of London in the late Victorian era was not merely a moral and political problem; it was a practical fact that shaped the criminal ecology of the city in specific and important ways. The desperate poverty of the slum districts produced a specific type of crime — opportunistic, often violent, directed primarily at the extraction of immediate economic value from whatever was available — and the perpetrators of this type of crime left behind a specific type of evidence and could be expected to pursue a specific range of subsequent actions. The relative prosperity of the middle-class districts produced a different ecology: the crimes of these areas were more calculated, more technical, and directed toward different kinds of value, and the perpetrators correspondingly left different evidence and pursued different subsequent courses of action.

At the intersection of these two ecologies — in the mixed districts where extreme wealth and extreme poverty existed in close proximity, as they do in many parts of London — the most interesting and in some ways the most dangerous forms of criminal enterprise developed, because these were the zones where the specific technical skills and social knowledge of the higher criminal type could be combined with the desperation and the direct violence of the lower. The confidence operator who used the desperate as instruments for the delivery of threats or the execution of physical operations while keeping his own hands clean; the fence who operated at the boundary between the legitimate and the criminal markets; the blackmailer who drew his leverage from the secrets of the wealthy and employed the desperate as his agents of delivery and enforcement — these types were characteristic of the social interface zones and presented the most complex investigative challenges.

My irregular agents — the Irregulars, as Watson has described them, and the various older informants and observers I maintained in the areas most relevant to my practice — were an essential resource in the investigation of crimes originating in or passing through these zones. The official investigators were at a systematic disadvantage in these areas precisely because the official presence was distrusted and the official enquiries produced, at best, silence and at worst misinformation. My agents, who were themselves part of the social fabric of these areas rather than external authorities descending upon it from outside, could gather information that was simply not available to the official channels.

The organisation of this informal intelligence network was itself a problem that rewarded systematic thought. The information gathered by agents operating at the margins of the criminal world has a particular character: it is often accurate in its specific, particular details and often inaccurate in its general framing, because the agent has observed a specific fact but has interpreted that fact through a lens of assumptions and expectations that may not be correct. The skill in managing such information is in the extraction of the specific factual content from the interpretive framework in which it is embedded — in asking not what the agent concluded from what they saw, but what exactly they saw. This distinction, between the observation and the inference from the observation, is fundamental to the use of any source of intelligence, however sophisticated or however crude.

I have found, over many years of working with informants of varying degrees of reliability and sophistication, that the most valuable are not necessarily the most intelligent or the most experienced, but the most scrupulously honest in their reporting — the ones who are content to describe what they actually observed without embellishing it with their own interpretive additions. Such informants are rarer than one might wish. The natural human tendency is to explain what one has seen, to place it in a context, to make it mean something, and the result is that the raw observational data is almost invariably mixed, in any account that an untrained observer gives, with the observer's interpretive overlay.

The training that I have given to the more capable of my irregular agents has focused precisely on this distinction: on teaching them to observe without immediately interpreting, to report without embellishing, to distinguish between what they saw and what they concluded from what they saw. This training has produced, in several cases, informants of genuine investigative value — people who have learned to look at the world with something approaching the systematic attention of the trained observer, and to report what they see with something approaching the scrupulous accuracy that the investigative enterprise requires.

The question of criminal psychology — of the specific mental states and processes that lead individuals to commit crimes — has occupied my attention at various points in my career, partly as a matter of direct professional necessity and partly as an extension of my general interest in the variety of human nature. My approach to criminal psychology has always been primarily inductive rather than theoretical: I have observed a large number of criminals, in a variety of circumstances and types of crime, and I have attempted to identify the patterns that recur with sufficient regularity to be useful for predictive and investigative purposes.

The most consistent pattern I have observed is the tendency of criminals of all types to underestimate the intelligence and thoroughness of those investigating them. This underestimation takes different forms in different types of criminal, but it is remarkably consistent: the sophisticated fraudster who has taken extraordinary care to conceal the technical details of their scheme will often fail to account for the possibility that the investigator has resources of knowledge or observation that they have not anticipated; the careful murderer who has managed the physical evidence of the crime with meticulous attention will often leave traces in the social and commercial record of the days surrounding the crime that they have not thought to conceal, because they have not recognised their investigative significance.

This consistent underestimation is one of the investigator's most reliable advantages, and it should not be squandered by permitting the criminal to form an accurate assessment of the investigator's methods and resources. There is practical value, therefore, in maintaining some degree of public obscurity about the specific methods and resources available to the investigator — in allowing the criminal community to hold an outdated and underestimated view of what the investigative science is capable of. This is one reason why I have been less than fully forthcoming, in the published accounts of my cases, about certain of the more advanced analytical techniques I employ.

The published accounts, as Watson has produced them, serve a different purpose from the professional treatises I have occasionally written for specialist audiences. Watson's narratives are addressed to the general reading public, and their principal purpose is the illustration of investigative principles through specific cases — the demonstration, by concrete example, of how the method of systematic observation and logical inference can be brought to bear on problems that appear, at the outset, to be insoluble. They serve this purpose tolerably well, though Watson's literary instincts lead him, in my judgement, to give somewhat too much weight to the dramatic and the sensational aspects of the cases at the expense of the methodological details that would be of greater interest and utility to the serious student of the investigative art.

I have on occasion suggested to Watson that his accounts would benefit from a more thorough exposition of the analytical processes by which the conclusions were reached, rather than the somewhat compressed and occasionally mysterious treatment of the reasoning that he typically provides. His response has been that the readers find the reasoning less interesting than the drama, and that a fully detailed analytical account of even the simplest inference chain would lose the general reader before the case had properly begun. There is probably something in this, as a judgement about the tastes of the general reading public; but it means that the published accounts, for all their value as popular narratives, do not fully serve the purpose of instruction in the investigative method.

The London winter, which I have always found more conducive to intensive thought than the warmer and more varied seasons, brought with it, in the years of my most active practice, a particular rhythm of professional life: the cases more numerous in the winter months, when the shorter days and the more confined domestic life of the population produced, it seemed, a higher frequency of the kinds of conflict and difficulty that led people to seek outside assistance; the intervals between cases more intense, the mind more active in the compensatory way that I have described. The long evenings with the violin, the long nights at the chemical bench, the systematic reading and the careful maintenance of the indexes — all of these had their proper place in the winter rhythm of Baker Street.

And then the bell would ring — the particular quality of ring that distinguished the anxious from the curious, the genuine case from the idle enquiry — and Watson would look up from his book or his writing, and Mrs. Hudson would be heard on the stairs, and a new narrative would begin. Each new case was, for me, both a professional engagement and an intellectual event: a new specific problem to be solved by the method I had spent my life developing, a new test of the principles I had worked to establish on a firm theoretical foundation, a new opportunity to advance, by however small an increment, the science of criminal investigation.

It is this combination of the practical and the theoretical — of the immediate specific problem and the general methodological principle — that has sustained my engagement with the work over so many years. The purely practical investigator, engaged only with the specific cases before him and without any interest in the general principles they illustrate, will find the work satisfying for a time but will eventually discover its limitations: the same types of problem recur, and without the theoretical framework that allows the general pattern to be identified and the specific variation to be placed in context, the recurrence will appear as repetition rather than as variation on a theme. The purely theoretical student of criminal investigation, who engages only with the general principles and never submits them to the test of specific practical application, will produce a system that is internally coherent but practically useless, because the specific problems of practice always contain complications and variations that the purely theoretical approach cannot anticipate.

The synthesis of the practical and the theoretical — the continuous movement between the specific case and the general principle, each informing and refining the other — is what I have aimed at throughout my career, and what I believe represents the most complete and most effective approach to the investigative enterprise. It is an approach that demands a breadth of knowledge and a flexibility of mind that are not commonly found together, which is perhaps why the approach, though I have described it clearly enough in my various published and unpublished accounts, has not been as widely adopted by practising investigators as its practical utility might lead one to expect.

But the method is sound. Of that, at least, I am entirely confident. And its soundness is demonstrated, every time it is properly applied, by the results it produces: the apparently inexplicable made explicable, the apparently invisible made visible, the truth established where before there was only confusion and darkness. That is the test of any method, and by that test the method is vindicated.

The fog over London had lifted by the time I turned from the window, and the pale winter sun had established itself with sufficient authority to make the familiar features of Baker Street clearly visible. The hansom cabs went about their business; the pedestrians went about theirs; the city, as always, went about the business of being a city — generating, in the process, its endless supply of human drama, human complexity, and human need. Somewhere in those streets, at that moment, a crime was being committed, or planned, or discovered; somewhere, someone was in trouble of the kind that would, in due course, bring them to my door.

I took up my pipe and my book, and I settled into the chair, and I waited. The waiting is part of the work. The case, when it came, would require everything I had: all the observation, all the analysis, all the knowledge accumulated over a lifetime of practice, all the patience and the method and the willingness to follow the evidence wherever it led. I was ready. I was, in the only sense that matters, always ready.



* * *

It is a truth universally acknowledged among those who have had occasion to study the science of deduction and analysis that the mind of the trained observer is an instrument of extraordinary precision, capable of extracting from the most apparently barren and unpromising collection of physical details a complete and coherent narrative of events that would otherwise remain impenetrable to the understanding of the casual or untrained witness. I have spent the better part of my adult life in the cultivation of this instrument, honing its edges against the whetstone of practical experience, subjecting its conclusions to the rigorous test of subsequent verification, and expanding its range through the systematic acquisition of knowledge in every field that bears, however remotely or indirectly, upon the investigation of human conduct and its physical consequences. The result of these labours is the method I have described on various occasions to my friend and associate Doctor Watson, and which I shall now attempt to set forth in somewhat greater detail and with somewhat greater theoretical rigour than I have hitherto found occasion to employ.

The foundation of the method is observation. Not the casual, habitual, half-attentive form of seeing that most human beings practice most of the time — the automatic visual processing that allows a person to navigate through their environment without colliding with the furniture, to recognise familiar faces and familiar places, to read the expressions of the people they encounter and adjust their behaviour accordingly — but the active, systematic, deliberate form of looking that refuses to accept the first interpretation of what is seen and demands instead a complete inventory of all the data available before proceeding to any interpretation at all. The difference between these two modes of visual engagement is enormous, and it is a difference that most people never discover because they never have occasion to exercise the second mode and therefore never become aware that the first mode is as limited as it is.

Consider what a person sees when they enter a room for the first time. They register the general character of the space — its size, its lighting, its degree of comfort or discomfort, its social register. They note the other people present and form rapid impressions of them based on appearance and demeanour. They identify the functional elements of the room — the chairs, the table, the door, the windows — and orient themselves in relation to them. This is what the ordinary person sees. This is approximately what I see in the first half-second of entering any room. In the subsequent seconds, while the ordinary person is beginning to engage with the social situation or the practical purpose that brought them to the room in the first place, I am conducting a survey of an entirely different order: cataloguing the specific objects visible and their precise arrangement, noting the evidences of recent use and recent occupation, observing the traces left by the room's inhabitants of their habits and their history and their present circumstances, reading the physical text of the space with the same systematic attention that a scholar brings to the reading of a manuscript.

The books on a man's shelves, for instance. These are among the most informative elements of any domestic or professional interior, and they repay careful study in ways that their owners seldom anticipate. The arrangement of the books tells you something: a collection arranged by subject speaks of a systematic mind, one arranged by size speaks of a mind that values appearance over utility, one arranged apparently at random speaks of a mind that knows its own collection well enough to find any given volume without relying on any formal system, or alternatively of a mind that has never developed the habit of systematic organisation. The specific titles tell you more: what a man chooses to read, and what he chooses to display among the things he reads, reveals his intellectual interests, his social pretensions, his professional concerns, and sometimes his hidden anxieties. A well-worn copy of a medical text on the shelf of a man who is not himself a medical professional suggests either a past illness of a serious nature in himself or in someone close to him, or a present anxiety about health that he has not mentioned. A collection of legal texts similarly interpreted. The books that are absent are sometimes as informative as those that are present: a man who has all the standard works on a given subject except the most recent and authoritative one is a man who stopped following the subject at a particular point, and the question of why he stopped is worth asking.

The desk tells you the nature of a person's work and the organisation of their mind. A clear desk is either the desk of a very orderly person or the desk of a person who has recently cleared it for some specific purpose, and the two possibilities are distinguishable by other evidences. The papers that are prominent on a working desk are the papers that the occupant was engaged with most recently, or that they consider most immediately important, and the former and the latter categories are not always the same, which is itself informative. The tools of the desk — the pens, the inkwells, the correspondence trays, the reference books immediately to hand — tell you what activities are regular and what are occasional. The wear on the chair and on the surface of the desk tells you where the occupant habitually sits and how they sit, and from this one can deduce the characteristic posture and from the posture a good deal about the physical character of the individual.

I have described these things in what may appear to be excessive detail, but the detail is not excessive — it is necessary. The method cannot be practiced in outline or in principle alone; it must be practiced in the specific and the particular, applied to the actual details of the actual room or the actual person or the actual document under examination. A student who has read and understood all the theoretical principles of the method but who has never trained the habit of actual observation will be of very limited practical utility, because the principles are merely the framework and the framework is empty without the substance of specific, accumulated observational experience.

The streets of London constitute the largest and most various field for the practice of systematic observation that I have ever encountered. In all my travels on the Continent and my periods of residence in various other cities, I have never found a place that offers the observer so many layers of human activity so densely compressed into so small a space. The London street, at any hour of the day, is a theatre of continuous human drama in which dozens of separate narratives are proceeding simultaneously, each with its own cast of characters, its own history and its own trajectory, and all of them intersecting and separating and intersecting again in the complex choreography of metropolitan life. To walk down Baker Street on a November morning and to see it as I see it — as a document to be read, a text to be interpreted — is to experience something that I find genuinely and continuously satisfying, in the way that a musician finds a complex and interesting piece of music genuinely and continuously satisfying: the pleasure of a faculty fully and appropriately engaged.

The approach to Baker Street from the north on a foggy morning presents a particular quality of scene that I have observed and reflected upon many times. The fog does not, as one might naively suppose, reduce the quantity of available information — it alters the nature of it, shifting the burden of observation from the visual to the auditory and to the other senses, and in doing so it sometimes makes available information that would otherwise be drowned out by the dominant visual channel. The sound of footsteps on wet pavement carries further and more distinctly in fog, and the trained ear can extract from the sound of a man's footsteps — their pace, their weight, their regularity or irregularity, the specific quality of heel-strike and toe-off — a set of inferences about the man's physical characteristics and current emotional state that rival in their informativeness what the eye might ordinarily extract from a direct visual observation.

The particular clay of the London streets, which varies in colour and composition from district to district in ways that a careful student can learn to identify with reasonable precision, adheres to footwear in patterns that are diagnostic of the areas through which a person has recently walked. I have developed, over many years of study and observation, a fairly comprehensive map of the geological and chemical variations in the street-mud of the principal areas of the metropolis, and I can often determine, from the traces of mud on a client's boots or trousers, not merely the general area from which they have come but the specific streets or even the specific stretch of pavement along which they have recently passed. This knowledge has proven of practical utility on more occasions than I can readily enumerate.

The coal-smoke that perpetually overhangs the city adds another layer of information, since the specific mixture of combustion products varies with the type of coal being burned and the type of furnace or fireplace in which it is burned, and different areas of the city and different types of establishment tend to use different coals. The characteristic smell of the commercial districts differs from that of the residential areas, and both differ from the smell of the areas where manufacturing is carried on. A person who carries on their clothing the distinctive odour of a particular type of industrial process has recently been in the vicinity of that process, and the information this provides, when combined with other observations, can be quite specific.

I do not propose to enumerate all the observational resources available to the trained investigator in the London street. The point I wish to make is simply that the city is not, as it appears to the casual observer, a confusing and largely unintelligible mass of undifferentiated humanity going about its business in a more or less random fashion. It is, to the trained observer, a continuous and detailed text, written in the common language of physical cause and effect, and legible to anyone who has taken the trouble to learn the language. The criminal who believes that the city's noise and confusion will conceal his activities is making a fundamental error. The city records everything. The question is only whether the right observer is present to read the record.



* * *

The Baker Street rooms in which I have conducted the greater part of my professional life represent, in their own way, a kind of autobiography — or at any rate, the physical expression of a mind and a character, the accumulated residue of thirty years of intellectual activity. Watson has described them, in his published accounts of our various cases, with considerable fidelity to their physical character if not always with complete accuracy in their symbolic meaning. He has noted the chemical bench with its stains and its array of apparatus; the deal-topped table where I conduct my experiments; the files and the indexes in which I have attempted to impose some order upon the vast accumulation of criminal and quasi-criminal knowledge that my profession has required me to assemble; the tobacco in the Persian slipper on the mantelpiece; the correspondence pinned to the centre of the chimney-piece with a jack-knife; the violin that represents my principal relaxation and my most reliable thinking-aid.

What Watson has been less successful in conveying, because it is less amenable to direct description, is the atmosphere of the rooms — the quality of concentrated thought that seems to me to have soaked into the fabric of the place during the long hours of analysis and ratiocination that have been conducted there. I am aware that this is a fanciful notion, that rooms do not literally absorb the mental activities of their occupants, that the atmosphere I perceive is a function of my own accumulated associations rather than of any quality inherent in the walls or the furniture. But the practical effect is real enough: in these rooms, my mind works better than it works anywhere else. The familiarity of the environment, the absence of competing stimuli, the comfort of the accustomed surroundings — all of these things permit a degree of concentration that is more difficult to achieve in less familiar or less controllable settings.

The chemical experiments that I conduct at the bench have been a source of considerable anxiety to Mrs. Hudson and of intermittent alarm to Watson, and I cannot claim that their anxiety and alarm have been entirely without foundation. There was the incident with the sulphuretted hydrogen, which might have been considerably more serious than it was, and the occasion when the experiment with the new reagent produced results that were surprising even to me and that temporarily altered the colour of the wallpaper in a manner that Mrs. Hudson found offensive. These episodes I regard as the inevitable accompaniments of serious experimental work, the price that must be paid for genuine inquiry; Mrs. Hudson and Watson regard them rather differently, and their views, though I do not share them, are not without a certain practical justification.

The experiments themselves have served two distinct purposes in my career. The first is the development and refinement of analytical techniques that I have subsequently applied to specific investigative problems — the various tests for different types of blood, the methods for distinguishing between the combustion products of different varieties of tobacco, the techniques for identifying the composition of various inks and papers that have been of service in cases involving the analysis of written documents. The second purpose is less immediately practical and harder to explain to those who have not experienced it: the experiments serve as a form of controlled intellectual engagement that maintains the acuity of the analytical faculties during the intervals between active cases, preventing the deterioration that I have observed to result from complete idleness of the intellect.

The violin serves a similar but distinguishable function. The experiments engage the analytical mind in the solution of specific technical problems; the violin engages something different — a mode of thought that is less explicitly logical and more intuitive, that processes information at a level below conscious articulation and sometimes produces, through this sideways route, insights that the directly analytical approach has failed to generate. I have on several occasions during a period of apparent musical improvisation — which Watson has described, perhaps not unfairly, as "rather desultory scraping" — arrived at solutions to problems that had resisted my most systematic direct analysis. The mechanism by which this occurs is not entirely clear to me, and I will not pretend that it is. I know only that it does occur, and that the knowledge of its occurrence makes the violin, for me, something considerably more than a hobby or a social accomplishment.

The criminal investigation is, in its essential structure, a problem of reconstruction. The investigator arrives at the scene of a crime — or arrives at the client's sitting room and receives a description of the relevant circumstances — after the fact, sometimes long after the fact, and must from the available traces of past events reconstruct what those events actually were. This is a fundamentally different kind of intellectual problem from the mathematical or logical puzzle, in which all the relevant information is presented at the outset and the task is simply to identify the relationships among the given elements. In the investigative problem, one does not know in advance what information is relevant, or whether the information one has is complete, or whether what appears to be information is in fact accurate. The investigator must simultaneously determine what questions to ask, gather the data required to answer them, assess the reliability of the data gathered, and construct from all of this a coherent account of what occurred.

It is this multi-dimensional quality of the investigative problem that makes it genuinely difficult — not merely technically complex but requiring a particular kind of intellectual flexibility, a willingness to entertain multiple hypotheses simultaneously while submitting each of them to the test of the available evidence, and a specific form of courage: the courage to abandon a hypothesis, however carefully constructed and however emotionally satisfying, when the evidence demonstrates that it is wrong.

I have worked with, or alongside, or in opposition to a considerable number of professional investigators over the course of my career, and I have observed in nearly all of them, to varying degrees, the fundamental weakness of the professional mind in this respect: the tendency to find the solution early and then to defend it rather than continue to test it. This tendency is understandable, and its origins are not difficult to identify. The professional investigator is under institutional and social pressure to produce results; the production of a suspect and the accumulation of evidence against that suspect is regarded as progress, while the continuing absence of a solution is regarded as failure; and the human mind, operating under these incentives, naturally tends to find solutions that can be defended rather than solutions that can be trusted.

The independent investigator — the man who has no institutional superiors to satisfy and no institutional reputation to protect, who is answerable only to the truth of the matter — is free from these pressures in a way that the professional is not. This freedom is one of the principal advantages of my particular position, and it is an advantage that I have consistently exploited. I have no need to be right before I am certain. I have no need to produce a suspect when I have only a hypothesis. I can take the time that the evidence requires, follow the trail where it actually leads rather than where it is convenient for it to lead, and arrive at conclusions that are genuinely supported by the evidence rather than merely consistent with the most accessible interpretation of part of it.

The London criminal world, which I have studied with something approaching the systematic thoroughness of the naturalist studying an ecosystem, has its own structure, its own hierarchies, its own internal logic. At the highest level — the level at which I have had, on various occasions, most cause to direct my attention — there are the great organisers: the men and women of intelligence and nerve who direct the activities of others without themselves engaging directly in any specific criminal act, who are therefore almost impossible to bring before a court by the ordinary means of evidence-gathering, and who are the most dangerous precisely because their insulation from direct criminal activity makes them immune to the ordinary processes of legal accountability. Below them are the specialists: the forgers, the poisoners, the safe-crackers, the confidence operators, each with their particular technical expertise and their particular market, operating sometimes independently and sometimes as components of larger criminal enterprises directed by the organisers. Below the specialists are the general practitioners: the burglars and pickpockets and fraudsters who lack the specific expertise of the specialists but make up for it in volume and versatility.

And below all of these are the desperate and the opportunistic — the people who commit crimes not as a profession or a vocation but as a response to immediate need or immediate passion, who constitute the largest proportion of the criminal population and the largest proportion of the cases that come before the courts, but who constitute only a small minority of the cases that come before me, because their crimes are generally of the type that the official machinery of investigation can handle without my assistance.

My practice has been concentrated, for the most part, at the upper levels of this hierarchy — in the cases where the intelligence of the criminal matches or approaches the intelligence of the investigator, where the physical evidence has been managed with sufficient care to prevent the ordinary methods from being effective, where the organisational complexity of the enterprise creates a complexity of evidence that requires more than routine analysis to interpret. These are the cases I find genuinely interesting. They are also, it must be said, the cases that are most important to resolve, since the crimes organised at the highest level of the criminal hierarchy produce the greatest aggregate harm — not always the most dramatic individual incidents, but the largest total of suffering and injustice distributed across the largest number of victims.

The fog over London on a winter evening has a particular quality that I have always found conducive to thought. The city sounds different in fog — the muffling of the distant sounds and the amplification of the near ones create a peculiar acoustic environment that narrows the effective radius of the social world, making the space immediately around one feel both more immediate and more isolated than the ordinary open-air environment. The gas-lamps in their fog-haloes produce a quality of light that is both sufficient for navigation and insufficient for detailed observation, which means that the foggy street forces upon the observer a reliance on the auditory and olfactory senses that is unusual in normal conditions and that, for the trained observer, reveals a different set of information from what the visual sense would normally dominate.

I have walked these streets at all hours and in all weathers, alone and in company, in the course of active investigations and in the course of what might be loosely described as recreation, which for me generally takes the form of observation for its own sake — the maintenance and extension of my knowledge of the city and its inhabitants, the constant updating of the mental map that I carry of London's criminal and near-criminal geography. These walks have contributed as much to my practical effectiveness as any amount of reading or laboratory work, because they have given me the kind of intimate, physical familiarity with the city that cannot be obtained from maps or books or any form of secondhand report, however accurate.



* * *

There are, in the practice of criminal investigation, certain recurrent types of problem that reward systematic study because they appear with sufficient frequency to make general observations useful. Among the most common of these is the case of the apparently missing person — the client who presents themselves at Baker Street with the account of a relative, a friend, or an associate who has disappeared under circumstances that the client finds inexplicable or suspicious. I have handled more cases of this type than I can readily enumerate, and the accumulated experience of these cases has taught me certain general principles that I apply, with appropriate modifications, to each new instance.

The first and most important principle is this: the circumstances of a disappearance are almost never truly inexplicable. Every disappearance has a cause, and the cause is almost invariably one of a limited number of categories. The person has left voluntarily, for reasons that they have chosen not to communicate to the person now reporting them missing. The person has met with an accident and is unable to communicate their whereabouts. The person has met with foul play of some kind. Or — a category that is more common than people sometimes suppose — the person is in the early stages of a mental disturbance that has temporarily disrupted their normal patterns of behaviour and communication without their being fully aware of the disruption themselves.

The first step in any missing person investigation is the determination of which of these categories applies, and this determination is often possible at the very first interview with the person reporting the disappearance, before any physical investigation has taken place. The key is the precise characterisation of the circumstances — not the emotional characterisation that the anxious reporter naturally tends to provide, but the specific physical and behavioural details that allow a trained observer to distinguish between the different categories.

A person who has left voluntarily has, in almost every case, left traces of preparation — traces that are often invisible to the person left behind precisely because they were designed, consciously or unconsciously, to be invisible, but that are apparent to the trained observer who knows what to look for. Certain items are absent from their usual places. Certain financial arrangements have been made in the days preceding the disappearance. Certain communications have been received or sent. Certain patterns of behaviour in the days preceding the disappearance have been unusual — unusual in ways that the person left behind noticed at the time but attributed to ordinary causes, and that only in retrospect, with the knowledge of the subsequent disappearance, acquire their true significance.

A person who has met with accident leaves a different set of traces — or rather, a different pattern of absences. The preparations that characterise the voluntary disappearance are absent. The last activities and movements of the person are consistent with their ordinary routine rather than with any form of departure. The place and time of the accident — if it can be located, which is not always immediately possible — will generally show evidence of the accidental event itself: physical signs of a fall or a collision or a sudden medical emergency, in a location consistent with the person's known movements.

A person who has met with foul play is a more complex and more serious matter, and the investigation of such cases requires, correspondingly, more thorough and more rigorous methods. The scene of the crime — if scene there be, and in many cases of foul play there is no single identifiable scene — must be examined with the greatest possible care and completeness, since the physical evidence available at the scene is typically the most direct and least ambiguous evidence available, before it has been contaminated by subsequent handling or disturbed by the passage of time.

I have made it a practice, in cases involving suspected foul play, to insist upon examining the relevant scene as early as possible and with as little prior disturbance as can be arranged. The scene of a crime is a document that deteriorates with time — not merely through the active contamination that results from the presence of multiple investigators and their various activities, but through the natural processes of physical degradation that begin to operate upon any physical evidence the moment the crime is committed and do not cease until the evidence is either preserved by some deliberate act or destroyed by time. The investigator who arrives at a scene twenty-four hours after the crime was committed is working with considerably less information than the one who arrives within an hour, and the difference is not always recoverable.

The footprint evidence, of which I have made considerable professional use, is particularly susceptible to deterioration. A footprint in soft earth or mud that is perfectly clear and detailed at the moment of its making will be measurably degraded within a few hours by the action of rain, wind, and the ordinary settling of the soil. The specific features of the print — the pattern of the sole, the depth and character of the heel-strike, the particulars of the toe-off — that allow the trained observer to extract information about the person who made the print are precisely the features that are most rapidly lost as the environmental conditions act upon the physical medium. I have accordingly developed the practice of making, at the very outset of any field investigation, a complete photographic and analytical record of all footprint evidence present at the scene, before proceeding to any other aspect of the examination.

The chemistry of the investigation extends beyond the laboratory and into the field. Many of the most important types of physical evidence are chemical in character — the traces of various substances on surfaces, in fabrics, on skin; the products of combustion that indicate the nature of the fuel burned and the conditions of the burning; the biological materials that can indicate the identity of the person who left them and the circumstances under which they were left. My training in analytical chemistry has been essential to my ability to identify and interpret this class of evidence, and I have spent considerable effort in recent years developing and refining techniques for the field analysis of chemical evidence that do not require the transport of samples to the laboratory.

The study of documents — their paper, their ink, their handwriting, their physical condition — constitutes another major branch of the investigative science, and one in which I have taken a particular professional interest. The physical characteristics of a document encode a great deal of information that is independent of the document's textual content: information about the period and place of the document's creation, about the instruments and materials used in its creation, about the physical history of the document since its creation, and about the conditions under which it was most recently handled. A letter that appears, on its face, to be a perfectly ordinary communication between two ordinary persons may, when its physical characteristics are properly examined, reveal that it was written on paper that was not commercially available at the time it purports to have been written, with ink that was not in common use in the country where it purports to have been written, by a person whose handwriting shows the characteristics of controlled simulation rather than the natural variation of spontaneous composition.

Forgery is a subject that repays careful study, both because it is in itself a common form of criminal enterprise and because the study of forgery illuminates, by contrast, the nature of genuine documents. The forger who works with skill and care is attempting to reproduce the appearance of authenticity — to create an object that will pass, upon examination, for something that it is not. To do this successfully, the forger must understand what genuine authenticity looks like — must know, that is, the specific physical characteristics that distinguish a genuine document of the purported type and period from an imitation. In attempting to reproduce these characteristics, the skilled forger demonstrates, paradoxically, that the characteristics themselves are real and specific and identifiable — because if they were not, there would be nothing specific to imitate. The forger's art is thus a kind of tribute to the reality of the physical evidences of authenticity, and the study of forgery is an indirect way of studying the nature of those evidences.

The art of disguise, which I have cultivated as a professional tool to an extent that Watson has occasionally found surprising, operates on similar principles. A convincing disguise is not merely a matter of altering the superficial features of appearance — the colour of the hair, the style of the beard, the cut of the clothing. It is a matter of inhabiting a different physical character: of adopting the posture, the gait, the characteristic gestures, the vocal qualities, and the social manners of the person being impersonated. The physical body is a document that the trained observer reads continuously, and a disguise that alters only the textual content while leaving the physical sub-text intact is a disguise that will not survive close examination by anyone who knows what to look for.

I have found, in the practice of disguise, that the most important element is not the alteration of the appearance but the alteration of the habitual self — the suppression of the physical habits and mannerisms that characterise one's normal presence and the substitution for them of the physical habits and mannerisms appropriate to the assumed identity. This is a more demanding exercise than is generally supposed, and it requires a kind of physical self-knowledge that most people have never had occasion to develop: the ability to observe one's own characteristic physical habits from the outside, as it were, and to consciously suppress and replace them.

The great city of London, in the years of my most active practice, was undergoing a transformation that was visible in the physical fabric of the streets as well as in the social composition of the population that inhabited them. The older buildings of an earlier century were being replaced, district by district, by the newer construction of the Victorian era: wider streets, more uniform building lines, better sanitation, and a general regularisation of the urban fabric that made the city more navigable but, in certain respects, less interesting to the close observer. The older, more irregular districts — the warrens of streets and courts and alleys that had grown up organically over centuries, without plan or systematic oversight — retained a complexity and a character that the newer development, for all its hygienic and practical advantages, could not entirely match.

I knew those older districts with an intimacy that I had acquired through years of deliberate exploration, and I found them consistently more informative than the newer, more regular areas of the city. The complexity of their geography mirrored, in some way, the complexity of their social life: they were places where the conventional social categories and the conventional social hierarchies were less rigorously enforced, where the established and the marginal, the respectable and the disreputable, existed in a closer and more complicated relationship than was possible in the more formally organised residential areas. And it was in these zones of social complexity that much of the most interesting criminal activity of the city was concentrated — not merely because they provided convenient cover, but because they existed at the intersection of social worlds that normally kept themselves separate, and criminal enterprise has always depended upon the exploitation of exactly that kind of intersection.

The professional criminal of the higher type — the organiser, the planner, the architect of extended schemes — tends to inhabit a social position that straddles the legitimate and the illegitimate, presenting a respectable face to the world while conducting, beneath that face, activities of a very different character. The perfect cover for a receiver of stolen goods is a legitimate dealer in second-hand goods; the perfect cover for a fraudster operating on a large scale is a position of genuine business respectability from which the fraudulent operations can be conducted under the shelter of the legitimate ones. The investigator who approaches such a person looking only for the criminal and ignoring the legitimate will often miss the evidence that matters, because it is in the relationship between the legitimate and the illegitimate operations — in the specific points of contact between the two, in the ways in which the criminal activity is concealed within or enabled by the legitimate one — that the most revealing evidence is typically to be found.



* * *

Watson has sometimes observed, with the gentle persistence that characterises his friendship, that my approach to the human beings involved in the cases I investigate is insufficiently attentive to their emotional experience. I understand his point, and I do not entirely dismiss it, though I think it reflects a misunderstanding of the nature of the investigative enterprise rather than a genuine deficiency in my character. The investigator's primary obligation is to the truth of what happened, and the emotional experience of the people involved, while it is part of the truth, is only part of it — and often not the part that most urgently requires attention.

There is, moreover, a practical reason for maintaining a degree of emotional distance from the specific situations under investigation: the investigator who becomes emotionally entangled with the circumstances of a case loses, to the extent of that entanglement, the objectivity that makes accurate analysis possible. I have seen this happen with other investigators — good men, conscientious and intelligent, whose emotional involvement with particular clients or particular situations led them to read the evidence in ways that served their emotional commitments rather than the truth, and to miss or minimise the evidence that pointed in uncomfortable directions. It is a consistent and serious professional failure, and it is one that I have worked consistently to avoid.

This does not mean that I am indifferent to the suffering of the people who come to me. On the contrary: it is precisely because I am not indifferent to their suffering that I maintain the discipline required to investigate their cases accurately rather than comfortingly. The person who needs the truth of their situation — the correct identification of the danger they face, the genuine assessment of the evidence against or for them, the accurate reconstruction of what actually happened rather than what they would prefer to have happened — is not well served by an investigator who has allowed his sympathies to cloud his judgement. They are served by an investigator who cares enough about their wellbeing to remain honest even when honesty is uncomfortable.

The cases that have tested this discipline most severely are those in which the truth, when discovered, is not what the client wished or expected. The wife who suspected her husband of fraud and was correct, but had not anticipated discovering that the fraud involved the systematic deception and financial ruin of people she knew and respected. The parent who feared that their child was in danger, and was correct, but had not anticipated that the danger was of a character that reflected very poorly on their own conduct as a parent. The business partner who suspected theft, and was correct, but had not anticipated that the theft was enabled by a flaw in their own practices that they had been systematically failing to address. In all of these cases, the truth, though it was the truth the client came to me to discover, was not entirely the truth they wanted.

I have developed, over the years, a certain technique for the delivery of unwelcome truths — a technique that involves neither the softening of the essential fact nor the unnecessary amplification of the painful elements, but the presentation of the truth in a context that makes its practical implications clear and that points, where possible, toward constructive responses. The truth delivered without context or without practical direction is a form of cruelty; the truth delivered with a clear account of what follows from it and what can be done in response to it is a form of genuine help. I aim for the latter, though I do not always achieve it to the degree that Watson's standards of human sympathy would require.

The observation of the human face is a science in itself, and one that I have studied with considerable thoroughness, though I have found that its results are less reliable than the observation of the physical environment or of physical objects, precisely because the face is the most consciously managed part of the human person's external presentation. People learn, from early childhood, to manage their facial expressions in response to social expectations — to display appropriate emotional responses and to suppress inappropriate ones — and the result is that the face, in social situations, reflects what the person believes they should be feeling or wishes to be seen as feeling at least as much as it reflects what they are actually feeling.

The more reliable indicators of the actual emotional and psychological state are, as I have noted, the hands and the body as a whole — the physical posture, the pattern of movement, the management of the breath and the muscular tension that are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and therefore not susceptible to the same degree of conscious management as the facial expression. A person who has trained themselves to maintain a perfectly controlled and socially appropriate facial expression will often betray, through the tightening of the hands on a handbag handle, or through the slightly increased rate and shallowness of the breathing, or through the particular way in which they hold their shoulders, the emotional reality that the face is working to conceal.
